steps.user_message: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves landlord-tenant eviction case. My lawyer is Robert Kim at Kim & Associates; we have proceedings at the civil division. We're in the early stages; our first hearing is next month.. Opposing party: the other parent in the custody case. This is in San Diego County, California. There are custody and support issues intertwined. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what questions the judge or opposing counsel might ask? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with legal-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Good — this is a smart, practical thing to prepare for. Below I’ve organized (1) focused questions to ask Robert Kim at your next meeting, (2) likely questions the judge or opposing counsel may ask you at the hearing (so you can rehearse concise answers), (3) a document/evidence checklist to bring, and (4) practical hearing tips and next steps. If you’d like, I can draft an email to Robert Kim with these questions and the case summary.

1) Questions to ask your attorney (Robert Kim)
- Case status & timeline
  - What is the exact procedural posture and what will happen at the first hearing next month?
  - What is our short-term plan and overall strategy (defend, delay, settle, counterclaim)?
  - What are best, likely, and worst-case outcomes for this stage?
- Procedural & logistical
  - What papers does the court expect us to file before the hearing? Are there local San Diego Civil Division rules/forms I should know about?
  - Do we need to exchange evidence or disclosures before the hearing? Deadlines?
  - Will you appear and speak for me at the hearing, or will I need to testify/answer the judge directly?
  - How long is the hearing likely to be? Can we request a continuance if we need more time?
- Evidence & witnesses
  - What evidence will be most persuasive for our position? What can we do now to strengthen it?
  - Which witnesses should we call? Do we need written declarations from them?
  - Should I prepare a witness list and marked exhibits? How many copies and formats do we need for court?
- Legal issues & defenses
  - What defenses are viable (e.g., improper service, lack of proper notice, habitability/repair, retaliation, discrimination, procedural defects)?
  - Are there counterclaims we should consider (e.g., unlawful eviction, damages for habitability)?
  - How might the custody/support matters intersect with this eviction case? Could evidence overlap or become admissible in both cases?
- Coordination with custody/support issues
  - Will anything I say at the eviction hearing risk negatively affecting the custody or support case? How do we protect sensitive information?
  - Should we notify the custody attorney (if different) about filings or testimony that might touch custody/support?
- Settlement & alternatives
  - Is mediation or settlement negotiation advisable now? What terms would be acceptable?
  - What are the likely costs vs. benefits of litigating vs. settling?
- Practical & billing
  - What will you need from me before the hearing and what are your fees for court appearances or extra work?
  - How should I communicate updates to you and how early do you need materials before the hearing?
- Preparation
  - Can we do a mock hearing or role-play probable questioning?
  - What exact language should I use if the judge asks me to state my position? (Ask for a short script.)
- Safety/confidentiality
  - If there are safety concerns with the opposing party (domestic issues), can the court accommodate (remote appearance, separate seating, protective orders)?

2) Questions the judge or opposing counsel are likely to ask (and how to prepare answers)
General guidance: keep answers short, factual, and on-point. Do not volunteer extra details; if unsure, say “I don’t recall” and consult your attorney.

Likely judge questions
- “Please state your name and your role in this case.” (Practice a clear one-line intro.)
- “What relief are you asking the court to grant today?” (Know your requested relief: dismissal, stay, more time, repairs, money damages, etc.)
- “Is there a written lease? When did the tenancy begin and who is on the lease?” (Have dates and names ready.)
- “Has proper notice been given? When and how were notices served?” (Know dates and proof-of-service.)
- “How much rent is owed (if any)? Do you dispute the amount?” (Bring rent ledger and receipts.)
- “Are there any safety or habitability issues?” (Be ready with concise facts, dates, photos, repair requests.)
- “Are you represented by counsel?” and “Do you consent to proceeding?” (Answer succinctly.)
- “Are you ready to proceed or do you need more time?” (Coordinate with attorney before answering.)
Likely questions from opposing counsel (adversarial)
- “When did you first fall behind on rent?” / “Why haven’t you paid?” (Stick to facts, avoid emotional statements.)
- “Did you receive the [3-day/30/60] notice? When?” (Tell dates and who served it; cite proof.)
- “Have you been told to leave before? Have you repaired the condition we allege?” (Respond factually.)
- “What is your relationship to the other party (the other parent)? Do they live in the unit?” (Answer truthfully but brief.)
- “Are there children living in the unit? How does this affect occupancy?” (Short factual answers.)
- “Did you make these electricity/repair/maintenance requests? Do you have proof?” (Reference exhibits.)
Potential cross-issue questions that could touch custody/support
- “Has there been any history of domestic incidents in this residence?” (If asked, consult attorney—be careful; it may affect custody.)
- “Is there a court order related to custody or child support presently in effect?” (Have the order ready; discuss answering with your lawyer.)

3) Documents and evidence checklist to bring to your attorney meeting and to the hearing
- Lease or rental agreement (full copy)
- Rent ledger / payment history (bank statements, cancelled checks, money order receipts)
- All written notices: eviction notice, 3-day/30-day/60-day, termination notices & proof of service
- Communication records: texts, emails, letters, messages with dates and sender/recipient
- Photographs or video of unit condition, repairs, damage, safety hazards (with timestamps if possible)
- Maintenance/repair requests and landlord responses
- Code-violation or inspection reports, habitability complaints to city/agency
- Police reports, incident reports, 911 call records (if any)
- Court orders from custody/support case and any pleadings or filings that relate to same parties
- Pay stubs, proof of income, proof of government benefits (if relevant to rent or support defenses)
- Witness contact information and short declarations/affidavits (if possible)
- Any prior settlement offers or agreements
- Government ID and a one-page timeline of the key events with dates (helps you testify concisely)
Bring paper copies (at least 2–3 sets) and digital versions. Label exhibits clearly and keep originals organized.

4) Practical hearing preparation & tips
- Prepare a one-page timeline (chronological) for your attorney and another short version to bring to court to reference.
- Practice concise answers to the likely judge questions above. Keep to 1–2 sentences.
- Role-play with your attorney: ask them to simulate questioning from both judge and opposing counsel.
- Do not argue with the other side in the hallway or in court—direct all communications through counsel or in court.
- If you don’t understand a question, ask the court to clarify: “Your Honor, could you please clarify?” or “May I answer through my attorney?”
- If there are safety concerns (fear of harassment), tell your attorney immediately so they can request accommodations.
- Make sure exhibits are pre-marked and filed if required by local rules; ask your attorney about required copies and exhibit numbering.
- Know whether the hearing will be in-person or remote and test any technology if remote.
- Keep emotions in check—the judge will rely on clear facts and documents.

5) Discovery and immediate actions you can take now
- Start assembling and backing up all documents and messages (print and digital).
- Create a dated timeline email or document that you can send to Robert Kim summarizing events — dates, names, key interactions.
- Ask your attorney whether to serve any discovery requests or subpoenas (e.g., for rent ledgers or maintenance records).
- If there are witnesses, ask them for short written statements now (signed and dated).
- Check for any local eviction moratoria, rental assistance programs, or San Diego-specific procedures that may affect timing.

6) Questions to ask yourself (to prepare clear answers)
- What exactly do I want the court to do at this hearing?
- What are the critical dates (lease start, notice served, missed payments, repairs, police calls, custody orders)?
- Who saw what happened and can corroborate it?
- Are there any court orders (custody/support) that I need to bring up or avoid discussing without counsel?

7) Next steps I recommend
- Schedule a focused meeting with Robert Kim ASAP to walk through the above questions and produce a short preparation plan for the hearing.
- Send him a one-page timeline and scanned copies of all key documents at least a week before the hearing.
- Ask him to do a mock hearing with you (10–20 minutes) to practice responses.
- Decide with your attorney whether to try mediation/settlement before the hearing.

If you’d like, I can:
- Draft an email to Robert Kim summarizing the case facts and listing the above questions and documents to send him; or
- Create a one-page timeline template you can fill in and print for the hearing; or
- Help you draft short, practice answers to each likely judge question.
